doc.title: Donn Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 6, 2009

title: After graduation: Army, Czech and the Washington scene
summary: Joining the Army language school, banjo at Monterey, Washington bands and the Federal Jazz Commission.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: And when you got out did you find other playing opportunities pretty steadily?

As a matter of fact no. After I got out in ’58 I found myself in a position of possibly being drafted. And so I joined the Army so I could go to the language school. And I did that, and I picked the language that I thought would land me in Germany, where I wanted to go, and they sent me to Fort Meade instead. So I ended up going to Fort Meade and then becoming a civilian at the same agency. And that’s where I worked for 38 years.
I see. You did a two year stint?
No three. When you enlisted you had to go for three but then you got three years of inactive reserve which meant I didn’t have to go to meetings. But in answer to your © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

question of whether or not I continued playing, well I had my banjo sent out to Monterey and the language I was taking, which was Czech, we had a little song session on Friday afternoon. And I would play the banjo and we had a bass player and another guitar player so we played along for Czech folk songs. But there was no opportunity for a band or anything like that. And when I got to the Washington area things were kind of in the doldrums which was in 1960, and I honestly cannot remember when my first paying gig occurred back in Maryland. I only remember who it was with. But things sort of came along, and musicians get to be known and then you’d have these big jam sessions and people will hire you or they’ll form a band. And we had a lot of small bands around in the seventies. And then I joined a band called Southern Comfort and then from there I went on assignment overseas and when I got back I joined the Federal Jazz Commission. But right after college no, there was nothing going on. In fact, because the music picture had changed in the public arena, in other words had gone to Bill Haley and that kind of music, even the Dixieland revival dried up in New York. And that was the end of that style of music. And I wasn’t about to join the Presley crowd.
